sysd-found-024.title: The OSI model: seven layers for talking about networks
sysd-found-024.text: Network engineers share a common vocabulary, and the OSI model supplied it. It is a logical, conceptual model that splits network communication into seven abstract layers, each stacked on the last. The layers run from sending bits across a physical medium up to the highest-level representation of data in a distributed application. Each layer has well-defined functions, serves the layer above it and is served by the layer below it. A protocol lets an entity in one host interact with the matching entity at the same layer in another host. Today's TCP/IP networks, described by the {{ref:sysd-found-029}}, do not implement the model directly. It still makes troubleshooting easier, and it encourages hardware makers to build products that can talk to each other. Thinking in layers also breaks a complex function into simpler parts and supports a security-first mindset.

sysd-found-029.title: The TCP/IP model: the Internet's four layers
sysd-found-029.text: Where the OSI model stacks seven layers, the TCP/IP model gets by with four: link, internet, transport and application. It sorts the Internet's protocols by scope and specifies how data is packetized, addressed, transmitted, routed and received. Its foundational protocols are {{ref:sysd-found-005}}, {{ref:sysd-found-015}} and {{ref:sysd-found-001}}. The link layer covers the local network, meaning every host reachable without crossing a router. The internet layer routes data between independent networks. The {{ref:sysd-found-030}} gives applications host-to-host data channels. The application layer holds protocols such as FTP, SMTP and DHCP, and leaves formatting and presentation to libraries and APIs. An application sends its data down through the layers, and each level encapsulates it further.

sysd-found-154.title: Clients ask, servers answer
sysd-found-154.text: In online banking, the browser asks a web server, and that web server acts as a client of the server that stores the data. An application server applies the business logic, and the web server returns the result. This is the client-server model: it splits the work of a distributed application between servers, which provide a resource or service, and clients, which request it. Clients start the conversation and servers wait for incoming requests. Whether a machine is a client, a server or both depends on the application. They exchange messages in a request-response pattern defined by an application-layer protocol, so the client only has to understand the response. Work runs on the server when it needs data or functions the client lacks, or would be slow, unreliable or insecure on the client. A server is often a central system serving many clients, and it is scaled beyond one machine with {{ref:sysd-blocks-112}} and {{ref:sysd-scale-058}}.

sysd-found-025.title: The seven OSI layers, from application to physical
sysd-found-025.text: From top to bottom, the seven layers are application, presentation, session, transport, network, data link and physical. The application layer is the only one that interacts directly with user data. It provides protocols such as {{ref:sysd-found-032}} and SMTP that browsers and email clients rely on, though the client software is not part of it. The presentation layer, also called the translation layer, handles translation, encryption and decryption, and compression of the application's data. The session layer opens and closes communication between two devices. It keeps a session open long enough to transfer all the data, synchronizes the transfer with checkpoints, then closes it promptly to avoid wasting resources. Layer 4, the {{ref:sysd-found-030}}, is responsible for end-to-end communication between two devices. It breaks data into segments and reassembles them on the receiving device. Just below it, the {{ref:sysd-found-031}} moves data between two different networks. It breaks segments into packets and finds the best physical path to the destination, which is called routing. The data link layer moves data between two devices on the same network, breaking packets into smaller pieces called frames. The physical layer covers equipment such as cables and switches. It converts data into a bit stream of 1s and 0s, with both devices agreeing on a signal convention.

sysd-found-030.title: The transport layer: from one application to another
sysd-found-030.text: The transport layer carries variable-length sequences of data from an application on a source host to an application on a destination host. Its protocols are either connection-oriented or connectionless. The layer below it imposes an MTU, a maximum packet size, so long streams are cut into segments small enough to leave room for the headers. Segmentation is optional. Connection-oriented protocols such as {{ref:sysd-found-005}} segment and reassemble data, while connectionless protocols such as {{ref:sysd-found-015}} usually do not. The layer can also control reliability through flow control, error control and acknowledgments. Protocols that keep state about a connection track segments and retransmit those that fail delivery. Reliability is not strictly required, though. Some protocols serve applications willing to accept packet loss, reordering, errors or duplication. TCP and UDP were not developed under the OSI model, but they are commonly categorized as layer 4 protocols.

sysd-found-019.title: Encapsulation: wrapping data in headers, layer by layer
sysd-found-019.text: Every layer of the network stack wraps the data it is given. Take data sent over {{ref:sysd-found-032}}. The application layer first adds a header of its own. At the transport layer a TCP or UDP header goes on, making a TCP segment whose header holds the source port, destination port and sequence number. The next layer down wraps the segment in an IP header with the source and destination addresses. At the data link layer the IP datagram gets a MAC header with source and destination MAC addresses. The resulting frames travel over the physical layer as binary bits. This nesting of a data payload inside a packet with a header is called encapsulation. The receiving device reverses it, removing the headers layer by layer until it can read the data. Each unit has its own name. A segment is the TCP protocol data unit, a datagram is the IP unit and a frame is the data link unit. The design works because each layer focuses on its own responsibilities. It relies on the headers for processing instructions and never needs to know what the data from the last layer means.

sysd-found-005.title: TCP: reliable, ordered delivery over an unreliable network
sysd-found-005.text: The Web, email, remote administration, file transfer and media streaming all rely on TCP. SSL/TLS often runs on top of it as well. TCP is one of the main protocols of the Internet. It provides reliable, ordered, error-checked delivery of a stream of bytes between applications on hosts communicating over an IP network. That is a bold promise, because the layers below may lose, duplicate or reorder IP packets. TCP detects those faults and requests retransmission of lost data. It rearranges data that arrives out of order and helps reduce network congestion. Every byte received is identical to what was sent, and in the same order. Before any data flows, sender and receiver establish a connection on agreed parameters through a three-way handshake. The application sees none of this. TCP hides the networking details behind a socket interface, the subject of {{ref:sysd-found-152}}. It splits the data into segments that are wrapped in IP datagrams and reassembled at the receiver. Reliability has a price: handshaking, retransmission and error detection all lengthen latency. TCP is optimized for accurate rather than timely delivery, with delays on the order of seconds. It is not particularly suitable for real-time applications such as voice over IP. Those can use {{ref:sysd-found-015}} instead, a connectionless datagram service that prioritizes time over reliability.

sysd-found-006.title: How TCP opens and closes a connection
sysd-found-006.text: Before a client can connect, the server has to be ready. It binds to a port and listens there, which is called a passive open. The client then makes an active open with a three-way handshake. It sends a SYN, the segment that asks to open a connection, carrying a random sequence number x. The server replies with a SYN-ACK that acknowledges x + 1 and carries its own random sequence number y. The client answers with an ACK holding sequence number x + 1 and acknowledgment number y + 1. Both sides have now received acknowledgments, and full-duplex communication, with data flowing both ways, is established. The cost is one round trip of latency before any data can be sent, which matters a lot for short flows. Closing takes a four-way handshake. An endpoint that wants to stop its half sends a FIN, and the other end acknowledges it with an ACK. A typical tear-down needs a FIN and ACK from each side. The side that sent the first FIN then waits out a timeout with the port unavailable, commonly 30 seconds, 1 minute or 2 minutes. That wait lets it resend the final ACK if it was lost. A host that closes a connection while unread incoming data remains sends an RST instead of a FIN. The received data is lost, and the RST tells the application so.

sysd-found-020.title: Common application-layer protocols and what each is for
sysd-found-020.text: Above the transport layer, protocols are standard methods of transferring data between two computers. The Web runs on a client-server protocol for fetching resources such as HTML documents, described in {{ref:sysd-found-032}}. Its encrypted extension is {{ref:sysd-found-048}}. Servers can push real-time updates over {{ref:sysd-msg-108}}, which gives full-duplex communication over TCP, while {{ref:sysd-msg-002}} always pulls. SMTP moves email from one user to another, and FTP moves files between client and server. Many of these build on TCP. {{ref:sysd-found-041}} describes a version whose transport relies on UDP instead, for faster page responsiveness.

sysd-found-001.title: IP: how packets find their way across networks
sysd-found-001.text: The Internet Protocol essentially establishes the Internet, because its routing function is what enables internetworking. IP is the network-layer protocol that relays datagrams across network boundaries. It delivers packets from the source host to the destination host based solely on the addresses in the packet headers. To do that, it defines packet structures that encapsulate the data to be delivered. It also defines addressing methods that label each datagram with source and destination information. Each datagram has a header, with the addresses and other metadata needed to route it, and a payload, which is the data being transported. The address space is divided into subnets by designating network prefixes, and addresses are assigned to host interfaces. All hosts and routers perform IP routing. A router's main function is to carry packets across network boundaries, and routers exchange routes with each other through routing protocols. IPv4, the first major version, is the dominant protocol of the Internet. Its successor, IPv6, has been in increasing deployment on the public Internet since around 2006.

sysd-found-021.title: IP addresses: labels that let devices be found
sysd-found-021.text: The Internet needs some way to tell computers, routers and websites apart, and the answer is the IP address. It is a numerical label assigned to a device on a network that uses the Internet Protocol, so that the device can be found and addressed. It does two jobs: identifying a network interface and giving that interface a location. An IPv4 address is 32 bits, which limits the address space to 4294967296 addresses. Some are reserved for special purposes such as private networks. People usually write one in dot-decimal notation: four decimal numbers from 0 to 255, each an 8-bit octet, separated by dots, as in 192.0.2.1. IANA and the five regional Internet registries manage the address space globally. They hand blocks on to local registries such as ISPs and large institutions. A host can even deduce the geographic position of a peer by looking its address up in geolocation data.

sysd-found-015.title: UDP: send the datagram and hope
sysd-found-015.text: UDP makes almost no promises, and that is its whole design. It is a core Internet protocol that sends messages, carried as datagrams in packets, to other hosts on an IP network. It is connectionless: there is no handshake or shared connection, and a host is not expected to keep track of what it has sent. A datagram is a header of four 2-byte fields (source port, destination port, length and checksum) followed by the payload. UDP does not guarantee delivery, indicate the original ordering or detect duplication, and it gives the sender no feedback. A program that wants reliability must build it, for example by adding its own confirmation that a message was received. The 16-bit length field sets a theoretical limit of 65,535 bytes for a datagram, and the actual limit for data over IPv4 is 65,507 bytes. Being connectionless, UDP can also broadcast to all devices on the subnet and support multicast, where one datagram is routed to a group of subscribers.

sysd-found-011.title: Port numbers: telling services apart on one address
sysd-found-011.text: One IP address can serve many services at once, and the port number is how traffic finds the right one. TCP uses 16-bit port numbers, so each port has 65,536 possible values. A connection is identified by a four-tuple: source address, source port, destination address and destination port. Well-known ports, 0 through 1023, are assigned by IANA to system-level processes. They include FTP (20 and 21), SSH (22), Telnet (23), SMTP (25), plain web traffic (80) and web traffic over SSL/TLS (443). On Unix-like systems, using one requires superuser permission. Registered ports run from 1024 to 49151. Dynamic or private ports (49152-65535) are commonly used as ephemeral ports for temporary client connections. On its public side, {{ref:sysd-found-028}} typically uses dynamic port numbers to tell apart traffic for many private hosts that share a single public address. Because a TCP connection's identity depends on addresses, it breaks if an endpoint's address changes.

sysd-found-152.title: Sockets: where programs meet the network
sysd-found-152.text: A socket address works like a phone number plus an extension. In TCP and UDP it is an IP address plus a port number. Internet sockets use it to deliver incoming packets to the right application process. A network socket is the software endpoint in a network node that sends and receives data, identified externally by its protocol, IP address and port number. It exists only for the lifetime of the application process, which gets a socket descriptor from the networking API. Stream sockets, usually TCP, give a reliable, ordered flow of data. Datagram sockets, using UDP, address and route each packet individually, with no guarantee of order or delivery. A server creates a socket in the listening state and waits for clients. A TCP server makes a dedicated socket for each client connection. Many of these can share one local address and port, because each socket pair has a unique 4-tuple. A UDP server socket has no established state and handles datagrams from every client.

sysd-found-018.title: IPv4 versus IPv6: running out of addresses
sysd-found-018.text: IPv4 is running out of room. Its 32-bit addresses, written as four dotted decimal numbers such as 192.168.0.12, allow approximately 4.3 billion unique addresses. The rapid exhaustion of that space led the IETF to redesign the Internet Protocol as IPv6. IPv6 uses 128-bit addresses, written as eight groups of four hexadecimal digits separated by colons. That gives up to approximately 3.403×10^38 addresses, deemed sufficient for the foreseeable future. The header changed too. IPv4's is more complex, with fields such as header length, header checksum and options. IPv6's is a simpler fixed 40 bytes, with rare fields in optional extension headers, which speeds packet processing. The two versions are in simultaneous use today. Dual stack runs both at once on the same devices, using whichever fits the destination address. One guide calls it one of the best approaches for a smooth transition.

sysd-found-016.title: TCP versus UDP: reliable but heavy, light but unreliable
sysd-found-016.text: TCP and UDP make opposite bets. TCP needs a handshake first: three packets set up a socket connection before any user data is sent, after which data may flow in both directions. It is reliable, managing acknowledgment, retransmission and timeouts. Either nothing is missing or, after multiple timeouts, the connection is dropped. It is also ordered, buffering out-of-order data until it can be delivered in sequence, though it is a byte stream with no signals marking message boundaries. All of that, plus congestion control, makes it heavyweight. UDP sends information in one direction without checking the receiver's readiness or state, and the sender cannot know whether a message arrives. There is no acknowledgment, retransmission or timeout. In return it is lightweight, sending packets individually with definite message boundaries, so one read at the receiver yields a whole message as it was sent. UDP does not avoid congestion itself, so the application or the network must handle that.

sysd-found-017.title: When UDP wins: voice, video, games and lookups
sysd-found-017.text: In a live voice or video stream, a late packet is worse than a lost one. That is why time-sensitive applications often use UDP: dropping packets is preferable to waiting for ones delayed by retransmission. Media streaming, real-time multiplayer games and VoIP are typical UDP applications. Loss of packets is not usually fatal, and in VoIP latency and jitter are the primary concerns. Video and audio protocols are designed to handle the occasional lost packet, so quality degrades slightly instead of suffering the large delays that retransmission would cause. DNS queries typically use UDP for its fast, lightweight nature, though DNS can also use TCP for large responses. Because UDP is stateless, it suits very large numbers of clients, as in IPTV streaming. Low-latency trading uses it to deliver market information to many recipients at once. One reliable and secure transport is built on UDP: {{ref:sysd-found-149}}. Web traffic carried over it needs a single handshake instead of the separate ones that TCP and TLS need.

sysd-found-002.title: Best-effort delivery: IP promises nothing
sysd-found-002.text: IP never promises that a packet will arrive. It provides only best-effort delivery: it is connectionless and unreliable, and the end hosts and upper-layer protocols must repair any faults. The Internet follows the end-to-end principle, which treats the network as unreliable at any single element or link and puts the intelligence in the end nodes. Data corruption, packet loss and duplication may all occur, and the end nodes must detect and compensate for each. Routing is dynamic and every packet is treated independently, so packets to the same destination may take different paths and arrive out of order. Upper-layer protocols resolve these reliability issues, for example when a host buffers network data so it reaches the application in the correct order. IPv4 does add one safeguard for the header. A routing node discards packets that fail the header checksum test, and it is not required to tell either end node. IPv6 has no header checksum.

sysd-found-007.title: How TCP notices lost data and resends it
sysd-found-007.text: TCP builds reliability on top of {{ref:sysd-found-002}} by numbering bytes and demanding receipts. A sequence number identifies each byte, so data can be rebuilt in order however it arrives. Receivers use the numbers to discard duplicates and reorder packets, and acknowledgments tell senders when to retransmit. An ACK says that data has arrived up to a specified byte. It does not mean the data reached the application, only that delivering it is now the receiver's responsibility. The sender keeps a timer for each packet and retransmits if it expires before an acknowledgment arrives. That timeout is one of two main ways TCP identifies loss. The other is duplicate cumulative acknowledgments: a lost segment makes the receiver repeat the acknowledgment for the last in-order packet. After three duplicates, the sender retransmits the last unacknowledged packet. The threshold is three because the network may reorder segments. After a timeout the sender retransmits and doubles the timeout, a pattern called {{ref:sysd-reliab-079}}.

sysd-found-009.title: Flow control: the receiver's window sets the pace
sysd-found-009.text: A fast sender can drown a slow receiver, such as a PC sending to a smartphone that processes data slowly. Flow control prevents that by keeping a TCP sender from sending data faster than the receiver can receive and process it reliably. TCP uses a sliding window. Each segment carries a receive window field that states how many more bytes the receiver will buffer. The sender may send only that much before it waits for an acknowledgment and a window update. When the receiver advertises a window of 0, the sender stops and starts a persist timer, which protects against deadlock if the window update is lost. A receiver that handles data in small increments may keep advertising a small window, a pattern called {{ref:sysd-found-165}}. The 16-bit window field is limited to 65,535 bytes, so the window scale option raises the maximum to 1 gigabyte for high-bandwidth networks. The option is sent only in the SYN segments during the handshake, with a value from 0 (no shift) to 14.
